How to coordinate property maintenance remotely

A repeatable loop for getting repairs done on a property you cannot visit, without overpaying or hoping for the best.

How-to · about 5 minutes

Remote maintenance fails in predictable ways: the problem is described vaguely, the price is whatever the first vendor says, nobody is there when the work is done, and "done" is a message rather than a photograph. The fix is a loop with five stages, each producing something you can see.

1. Describe the problem with evidence

A photograph of the leak, a short video of the sound, a note on when it happens. "Bathroom tap leaking" produces a plumber with the wrong part. "Hot-water tap in the master bathroom drips continuously; started after the geyser was serviced; photo attached" produces the right one, once.

2. Get a quotation, in writing, before work

Even a small job deserves a line that says what will be done and what it will cost, including materials. For anything above the amount you have set as your approval limit, get a second quotation. Vendors in Chennai will usually give a verbal estimate; ask for it typed into a message so it can be compared later with the bill.

3. Approve clearly

Reply with "approved, up to the quoted amount" or "not now". If you want to change the scope, say exactly what. Approvals buried in a long WhatsApp thread get lost; a short, explicit message is what the person coordinating needs to show the vendor.

4. Someone is present

Whoever lets the vendor in should stay, watch, and check the work before the vendor leaves. For plumbing: run the water. For electrical: switch everything on. For painting: look in daylight. This is the stage that most often gets skipped when a relative is helping, and it is the one that prevents the second visit.

5. Completion evidence and the bill

Photographs of the finished work, the bill, and a note of any warranty the vendor offers. File all of it against the property. When the same tap fails again in eight months, you will want to know who fixed it and what they were paid.

Setting an approval limit

Choose an amount below which routine work may proceed without asking you, and a separate, usually higher, amount for genuine emergencies. The point is not the figure; it is that small jobs do not wait for a time-zone round trip, and large ones never happen without you.

What counts as an emergency

  • Water leaking into another flat or from the flat above
  • Electrical burning smell, sparking, or a main that will not stay on
  • A lock that will not secure the door
  • Gas smell

Everything else can wait for a quotation.

If a service is coordinating maintenance for you, ask how they are paid: a management fee that is separate from vendor charges, with quotations passed to you as received, keeps their interest and yours aligned.
